content.intro: This lesson covers Swarm Security and Access. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Treat an image and its runtime settings as part of the security boundary. Use maintained image bases, non-root execution where possible, minimal capabilities, constrained mounts and networks, secret-safe build mechanisms, and vulnerability/component review. Docker daemon access itself is privileged. Learning swarm security and access helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

items.title: Secret handling
items.text: A secret needs a restricted path from its source to the process that needs it. Avoid putting it in images, normal build arguments, source control, or diagnostic output.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
